qs.q: Which of the following would cause an increase in both glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renal plasma flow (RPF)?
qs.e: Afferent arteriole dilation increases both blood flow into the glomerulus (increasing RPF) and glomerular capillary pressure (increasing GFR). This is the only option that increases both parameters.

qs.q: Which change increases both renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate?
qs.e: Afferent arteriolar dilation increases blood flow into the glomerulus and raises glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, increasing both renal plasma flow and GFR.

qs.q: Glomerular filtration rate would be increased by
o: A decrease in renal blood flow
A decrease in afferent arteriolar pressure
A decrease in the concentration of plasma protein
qs.e: Decreased plasma protein concentration reduces oncotic pressure, decreasing the force opposing filtration and thereby increasing GFR.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: GFR measures how much plasma the kidneys filter each minute. It reflects overall kidney health and guides diagnosis, staging, and treatment of renal disease.

sections.p: GFR is the volume of plasma cleared of waste per minute by the glomeruli. Normal adult GFR is ~90–120 mL/min/1.73 m²; it declines with age.
b: Low GFR → accumulation of urea, creatinine, fluid overload
High GFR may be seen in early diabetes or pregnancy

sections.p: Blood enters the glomerular capillaries under high pressure; filtration occurs across the fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte slit diaphragm into Bowman's space.
b: Filtration fraction ≈ 20 % of renal plasma flow
Starling forces (hydrostatic vs oncotic) drive filtration

sections.p: Autoregulation keeps GFR stable despite blood pressure changes via afferent arteriolar tone (myogenic response) and tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa).
b: Angiotensin II constricts efferent arteriole → raises glomerular pressure
Prostaglandins dilate afferent arteriole → protect GFR

sections.p: Reduced GFR signals kidney injury. Causes are grouped by location: pre‑renal (hypoperfusion), intrinsic (glomerular, tubular, interstitial), post‑renal (obstruction).
b: Pre‑renal: dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, hepatorenal syndrome
Intrinsic glomerular: diabetic nephropathy, lupus, post‑infectious GN, HIV‑associated nephropathy, schistosomiasis
Intrinsic tubular: acute tubular necrosis from toxins, severe malaria, contrast, rhabdomyolysis
Post‑renal: obstructive stones, prostate hypertrophy, congenital anomalies

sections.p: GFR guides staging of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and dosing of renally cleared drugs. Sudden falls define AKI (KDIGO criteria).
b: CKD stages 1–5 based on eGFR thresholds
AKI: increase in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 h or ≥1.5× baseline in 7 d

t.b: What is the current filtration capacity? Elevated creatinine suggests reduced GFR; use equations (eGFR) for estimation.
When is creatinine unreliable? Provides GFR estimate independent of muscle mass; useful in malnutrition or extremes of age.
Is there acute renal failure? <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 h signals AKI; monitor closely when labs unavailable.

faq.q: Why is creatinine not perfect for GFR?
faq.a: It varies with muscle mass, diet, and tubular secretion, so it can misrepresent true filtration.
